summary: This informational document defines terminology for benchmarking devices that control traffic by classifying packets on defined criteria. The terminology applies to data plane measurements. Classification rules can use any IP header field, such as the DSCP, or payload fields such as port number.

plainLanguage.summary: Before you can fairly compare two traffic cops, everyone must use the same words for what they measure. This document sets out those shared words.

questions: how to measure device congestion behavior
subtitle: Standard words for measuring how well network devices control traffic when links get congested.

tldr.problem: Network traffic control devices are hard to compare fairly because engineers use different definitions for the same measurements. Without shared terminology, it is impossible to benchmark and compare different traffic control systems.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a consistent set of terms for measuring traffic control device performance during congestion. It covers configuration terms (classification, flow), measurement terms (forwarding capacity, delay, jitter), and vector definitions that describe traffic in and out of devices under test.
tldr.outcome: Engineers can now use standard terminology to describe how traffic control devices handle congestion, making it possible to fairly compare performance across different vendors and systems.

facts.label: Measurement point
facts.value: Both ingress and egress interfaces of device under test

facts.label: Key distinction from older terms
facts.value: Measures egress behavior under congestion, not just ingress

facts.label: Delay measurement
facts.value: From last bit in to last bit out (LILO method)

today: RFC 4689 is an Informational RFC that provides standard benchmarking terminology for network device testing. It remains the reference for how to talk about traffic control device behavior during congestion.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Most existing benchmark terminology assumes that devices have plenty of capacity and do not experience congestion. But in the real world, devices often receive more traffic than they can forward, and new measurements are needed to understand how they behave under that pressure. This RFC introduces terminology designed specifically for measuring device behavior during periods when traffic exceeds capacity.

The key innovation is to measure traffic at both the input and output (ingress and egress) of a device, rather than just at the input. By watching what leaves a device under heavy load, not just what enters it, engineers can see whether congestion controls are working effectively.
sections.plainLanguage: This is about measuring what happens when traffic jams occur. We need words for describing how much traffic goes in, how much comes out, how long packets wait, and whether they all arrive in the right order.

sections.title: Configuration and Classification Terms
sections.content:
The document defines terms for how traffic control works. Classification is the process of sorting packets according to rules, such as looking at their source address, destination address, or a special marking called the DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point). Different traffic classes can be treated differently by Congestion Management, which uses mechanisms like traffic shaping or dropping to avoid or minimize congestion.

A Flow is a group of packets that all enter the device on the same input interface and leave on the same output interface. These flows can be tracked and measured separately, allowing engineers to see how well each traffic class is served.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic gets sorted into groups by rules (like sorting mail by destination). Different groups can be treated differently when the network gets busy. A flow is just packets going from one door to another door of the device.

sections.title: Key Measurement Terms
sections.content:
Forwarding Capacity is the maximum number of packets per second a device can transmit to the correct output interface without dropping any packets. This is different from the older concept of throughput, which only measures packets entering the device and does not account for queuing inside.

Forwarding Delay is the time from when the last bit of a packet enters the device to when the last bit of that same packet exits. Jitter is the variation in forwarding delay between consecutive packets. These measurements reveal the internal buffering and processing behavior of the device.

A Conforming Packet is one that stays within expected bounds for rate, delay, or jitter, while a Nonconforming Packet is one that exceeds those bounds.
sections.plainLanguage: Forwarding Capacity is the speed limit - the most packets per second that can leave without dropping any. Delay is how long a packet waits inside. Jitter is when some packets wait much longer than others. Conforming means the packet behaved as expected; nonconforming means it did not.

sections.title: Vectors: Describing Traffic in and out
sections.content:
A Vector is a description of a stream of packets that all share a particular classification marking or source-destination pair. Vectors describe both what is offered to the device and what comes out.

The Offered Vector describes the attempted rate of traffic sent to the device. The Forwarding Vector describes what rate of traffic actually leaves the device successfully. The Expected Vector describes what the test engineer predicts should come out, based on how the device is configured.

The document defines many specialized vectors for delay, jitter, and packet loss, each one measuring a specific aspect of how the device handles a particular traffic class under load.
sections.plainLanguage: A vector is like a label on a group of packets: it says what traffic class they are and what rate they were supposed to come out at. By comparing what was supposed to happen (expected vector) with what really happened (forwarding vector), engineers see if the device's traffic control is working.

sections.title: Tracking Packet Order and Loss
sections.content:
To measure whether packets arrive in the correct order, the RFC introduces the concept of a Test Sequence Number embedded in each test packet. A Stream is a group of packets that share common properties and are tracked together by a sequence number.

An In-Sequence Packet is one that arrives with the expected sequence number, showing the device did not reorder it. An Out-of-Order Packet is one that arrives with a sequence number lower than a previously received packet, indicating the device reordered traffic. A Duplicate Packet is one with the same sequence number as a packet already received, showing the device forwarded it twice.

These measurements matter because some applications, like streaming video or voice, become unusable if packets are reordered or duplicated.
sections.plainLanguage: Each test packet gets a number so we can see what order they arrive in. Some come out in order, some come out of order, and some arrive twice by mistake. Reordering and duplicates are problems for some applications.
